messages.subject: bias uncertainty
messages.body_plain:
Dear distance sampling group,

I’m coming up with a question not specific to Distance Sampling, but related. I guess that this is the correct forum for that and you could help me.

I’m estimating bias on density. I have the reference density (true) and a predicted density (potentially biased). I’m estimating bias with the formula:

Bias = (predicted density – reference density)/reference density

And I would like to ask if it is possible to estimate, somehow, the uncertainty of the bias. Thus, we can also assess how the confidence interval of the bias overlaps with 0 (ie. True density = predicted density).

All that I propose was using bootstrapping. Thus, from the mean and standard error of the density, I simulated a set of values (lognormal distributed); we then estimated the bias; and we finally apply a non-parametric bootstrap to estimate the uncertainty of bias. Find the code below.

However, I’m not sure if this approach is statistically correct; and/or if there are other analytical procedures for that proposal.

Thanks a lot

Pablo

R code:

# working data. Let assume a population in which the true density is 5ind/km2
# and the predicted density (using imported movement data) is 10ind/km2

# data
obsvdens <- 5
SEobsvdens <- 1.1

preddens <- 10
SEpreddens <- 2

# simulate a set of 1000 values (assuming lognormal distribution) from mean and SE
obsv <- rlnorm(1000, log(obsvdens), log(SEobsvdens))
pred <- rlnorm (1000, log(preddens), log(SEpreddens))

# estimate bias
bias <- (pred-obsv)/obsv

# non-parametric bootstrapping with replacement
SEboot <- sd(sample(bias, replace = TRUE, 999))/sqrt(length(bias)); SEboot

Hi Eric,

you are right, I apologise for the poor explanation.

My true value is indeed an estimated density, which is considered as the true (reference). Specifically, in a set of populations in which I estimated the population density ("obsvdens"), I'm exploring what bias would have emerged if I use some parameters from other populations ("preddens").

Simple example: let's say that I applied CTDS in a given area for a given species, and I obtained density by estimating all the needed parameters (named detection distances, activity level, effort, etc) for the sampled population. Now, aiming to explore the bias when importing some parameters from other populations (eg. the activity level - availability for detection); I estimated again the density by using the activity level from the literature (and assuming constant the other parameters: distances, encounter rate, effort...).

Thus, I have the "obsvdens" and it uncertainty (which I assumed the true), and the predicted density "preddens" and its uncertainty when using the activity level from other population. From these two values, I estimated the bias, which is very useful to show the equivalence (or not) of both estimates.

While the point estimate will reflect the mean bias in density, I'm wondering how can I show the overlapping (or not) between the uncertainties

Hope that my explanation is more clear now

Thanks a lot
Best
Pablo

No problem Pablo.

You're examining the difference between two estimates. Yes, your bootstrap approach seems appropriate. It is parametric because it assumes log-normal distributions for both estimates.

Rather than computing the standard error of the differences, why not compute a percentile confidence interval on the difference? Here are a few added lines to your code:

hist(bias, nc=50)
alpha <- 0.05
bounds <- quantile(bias, prob=c(alpha/2, 1-alpha/2))
abline(v=mean(bias), lwd=2)
abline(v=bounds, lty=3)
bmessage <- paste("Lower bound=", round(bounds[1],3), "\n",
                  "Upper bound=", round(bounds[2],3))
text(8, 100, bmessage)

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] No observations on a transect
messages.body_plain:
Casolyn

Under no circumstances should you remove transects (and effort) from your data if there are no detections on transects.  This will lead to gross over-estimates of abundance because the software will assume pigeons were detected on every transect you visited (because you removed transects when pigeons were not detected).

For transects without detections, you record everything about the transect, its label, the amount of effort, but for distance from transect, you set that value to "NA" if you are using the R package. If using Distance for Windows, leave the distance field blank when importing your data.

This would be the outcome if a flat (horizontal) detection function resulted from analysis of these data (which seems quite likely). messages.body_plain:
Casolyn

Looks like you are making good progress with your investigation. The histogram and QQ plot you provide are enlightening. The QQ plot specifically shows that the predominant lack of fit is at small distances. You might also plot your histogram of observed distances with many more distance bins—it appears that you have a large number of detections, so a more fine-grained histogram might show the source of the fit problems (although plots do not fix the problems). If the lack of fit is at small distances, truncation (removing detections at large distances) will have no effect upon fit.

"Spikes" in the histogram at small distances are notoriously difficult to deal with. Such data can arise from rounding perpendicular distances to 0 or observers trying to "guard" the transect by devoting too much effort to watching the transect. There is little to be done about this at the analysis stage.

You may need to make inference from a detection function that fails to adequately fit the data. You will need to note this threat to your inference in the report you produce.

messages.body_plain:
Riccardo

Accurate estimation distances from object to transect requires knowledge not only of where the animal is located, but also where the line is located.

The manual way of determining bearing to animal from the line in the field is to stand where the detection was made, face the direction of the transect (implying you know the bearing of the transect), determine the deflection from the direction of the transect to the direction of the animal. Shipboard survey folk use angle boards to determine deflection (degrees off the bow)

You could conjure something similar for terrestrial surveys.

Very similar suggestions can be found in Section 7.4.2 (Angle measurement) in Buckland et al. (2001).

Given you do not know the coordinates of the object, you cannot compute the shortest distance between the (unknown coordinate) object and the transect line.

If you have a field size​ in your data, then you have surveyed animals that occur in groups (or clusters). In this situation, the software will produce a density of groups. It will convert density of groups into density of individuals (individual animals).  How it makes the conversion depends upon how you have done your analysis.

In most situations, interest is in the number of individuals in the population. But this depends upon your study objectives.

The messages are warnings, not errors. Warnings are issued when the software does things (fitting models) about which it is uncomfortable. Granted software does not have feelings, but if it did, it would sometimes be "uncomfortable".

In the first instance (not strictly monotonic) the software has fitted a detection function where detection probability increases as a function of distance over some range of distances. The software is alerting you to this, suggesting you make the determination regarding the appropriateness of a detection function with this shape.

The second warning (hazard rate scale parameter very small) is issued when the software fits a detection function that falls off very rapidly with distance. As the message notes, this may be caused by data with a spike (many detections) at very small distances. You showed a histogram of detection distances that looked like this in your email on Wednesday. Again, the software is asking you to make a determination as to whether a detection function of this shape is biologically plausible.

Use AIC as a guide in model selection, it is not the only factor to be used in model selection.

Yes, that is correct.  Jo, more details below, which will be more than most will want to know!

You can consider how a count at a given point would be converted to a density estimate.  By dividing the point count by the effective area, you get estimated density.  Another way to view this is to divide the point count by estimated probability of detection, which gives an estimate of abundance at the circle of radius w about that point, where w is the truncation distance – detected animals beyond w are not included in the count.  Then to get from that abundance estimate to a density estimate, you divide by the area of the circle.  At least this is the case when the point is surveyed just once.  If it is visited say t times, you would divide the count by t, to get the mean count per visit.

The issue now is that we don’t have a good error model for the estimated densities at each point, but we do have suitable models for counts – e.g. Poisson or negative binomial.  So instead of taking the estimated density as the response, we take the count, and put the terms to convert it to a density estimate onto the right hand side of the equation model, as a so-called offset.  This only works if we us a GLM with a log link function - and the offset is actually the log of the terms taken onto the RHS, and is included in the exponent:  E(n)=exp(linear predictor + offset)).  In most applications, the offset would be known, but we only have an estimate of it.  We handled that by propagating the uncertainty in estimating probability of detection through to the count model, using a bootstrap.  Mark Bravington came up with a more sophisticated and less computer-intensive way to achieve the same thing.  Or you can be Bayesian, and estimate the offset along with the count model parameters in a single step.

Steve

When you say "hotspot" I presume you mean a concentration of pigeons at some distance from the transect. If so, this violates the so-called "design assumption" of distance sampling (Buckland et al. (2015:12)

> we assume that animals are distributed uniformly with respect to distance from the line (so that π(x) = 1/w) for line transect sampling
This is accomplished by a) random line placement and b) sufficient spatially replicated transects.  I recall mentioning in an earlier email exchange the challenge of random transect placement when sampling an urban environement.

Your historgram is labelled TD3; I don't know if that refers to a single transect; if so, you see the difficulty in adhering to the uniform distribution of animals in a single transect—animal aggregations can cause the uniformity assumption to be violated.

This problem cannot be solved by further modelling of the detection function or truncation (because the problem is not the result of the detection process). Modelling and estimation over larger spatial areas (with multiple transects) may ease the problem.

If the ‘hotspots’ are a result of coherent pigeon flocks, then the flock can be treated as the detection, and flock size recorded as ‘cluster size’.  That will reduce this issue.  But as Eric notes, given that you can’t follow random tracklines in urban environments, they may always be a lack of detections along the line, and goodness-of-fit tests will not give a reliable guide to whether a detection function model is suitable.

For pigeons, there would also be the issue of how to record flying birds.  If you include them, at the distance you detect them, that generates positive bias in estimates, because the distances will be biased towards small distances from the line, when flying birds are more likely to be detected.  You might need to exclude them from analyses, and separately estimate the proportion of pigeons that would be flying at any given time (probably small), and then adjust your estimate for flying birds.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Camera trap distance sampling related
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I have a camera trap sampled data set aimed at estimating the density of two group-living ungulate species, spotted deer and wild pig. The sampling was done with the objective to test Random Encounter Model in the study area. As parameters for REM analysis I have, a) distance and angle measured for animals that triggered the camera (initial trigger), b) speed estimates from image sequences where movement happened across at least two frames (trigonometrically estimated from measured distances and angles of animals subsequent to initial trigger), and c) count of the total number of animals of a species captured in each frame.

I have used Reconyx Hyperfire camera traps which were set to function 24hrs. At every motion-triggered event, the cameras recorded ten continuous images at a frame rate of 1 per second and were ready to trigger immediately again without delay.

Can I use this data set to estimate the density of these two group-living species following the camera trap distance sampling (CTDS) approach?

Just to reiterate, I have distances and angles measured, for every animal which triggered the camera, and only for those which have generated a movement sequence, but not for all the animals which were otherwise present in an image (those which neither triggered the camera nor contributed in movement sequence).

My queries are.

a) Does CTDS analysis require distances of every animal captured in the frame, irrespective of whether it triggered the camera or not?

b) What would be the number of observations (n) for these two group-living species?

c) Will an estimate for temporal availability for detection (activity level) be needed for density estimation of species which is always available for triggering the camera traps?

Sudip

messages.body_plain:
I think the problem you face is that your data were not collected with CTDS in mind. By using only distances to animals when they first triggered the camera, CTDS methods would give biased estimates. That is why CTDS needs distances at nominal snapshot moments which are separated by very short time intervals, so animals cannot pass right through the detection sector between one snapshot moment and the next. It sounds like you could use a time separation of one second or 2 seconds from your description. If you chose 1 sec, then effort would be number of seconds that the camera was operating. You would then need to estimate distance to each animal detected at each snapshot moment. So if an animal was visible in 7 successive images, you would need to include it 7 times, with 7 estimated distances. A longer interval between snapshot moments (say 5 sec) would reduce the work required, but if you make the interval too long, you will start to get bias again. Eric is correct in saying you would need to record each individual animal. You’ll see overdispersion in the data, so the analysis must be robust to this. See the Howe et al papers of 2017 and 2019.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Region label as a formula
messages.body_plain:
Aditya

When you have multiple regions (strata) identified in your data, the ds()​ function will produce estimates for each region, as you note. Those estimates will be calculated differently depending upon the presence of Region.Label​ in the formula argument. If there is no formula argument, then a pooled detection function is used to estimate region-specific estimates. If formula=Region.Label​ is included in the call to ds()​, then region-specific detection functions are created by using region as a covariate in the detection function.

Those two models can be compared using AIC to determine which is more appropriate for the data.

Plotting the detection function(s) arising from using Region.Label as a covariate can be accomplished calling the function add_df_covar_line​ twice (with separate values of Region.Label​) after calling the plot function.

Simple example using the minke​ data set shipped with the Distance package:

library(Distance)
data(minke)
reg_covariate <- ds(minke, key="hr", formula=~Region.Label, truncation=1.5)
plot(reg_covariate, main="Region as covariate")
regions <- unique(minke$Region.Label)
add_df_covar_line(reg_covariate, data=data.frame(Region.Label=regions[1]),
                  col="blue", lwd=3)
add_df_covar_line(reg_covariate, data=data.frame(Region.Label=regions[2]),
                  col="gold", lwd=3)
legend("topright", legend=regions, col=c("blue", "gold"), lwd=3)
